parts.label: a
parts.text: Use L’Hôpital’s rule to find the value of \(k\) for which \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 0\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the Maclaurin series for \(\cos x\) to show that, for \(x \neq 0\), \(f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{x^2}{24} + \dfrac{x^4}{720} - \ldots\)
For the rest of the question, \(k\) takes the value found in part (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the series in part (b) to find \(f'(0)\) from first principles.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f(x) - \frac{1}{2}}{x^2}\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Given that the series in part (b) is the Maclaurin series of \(f\), write down the value of \(f''(0)\).

parts.label: f
parts.text: By considering \(g(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{2} - 1 + \cos x\) for \(x \geq 0\), show that \(f(x) \leq \dfrac{1}{2}\) for all real \(x\).

idea: Continuity at 0 needs \(f(0)\) to equal the limit. Dividing the series for \(1 - \cos x\) by \(x^2\) gives a series for \(f\), which answers every later part: \(f'(0)\) is a limit of a difference quotient, and the coefficient of \(x^2\) in a Maclaurin series is \(\dfrac{f''(0)}{2}\).

solution.label: f
steps: \(g(0) = 0\) and \(g'(x) = x - \sin x \geq 0\) for \(x \geq 0\) (since \(\sin x \leq x\) there), so \(g(x) \geq 0\) for \(x \geq 0\): \(1 - \cos x \leq \dfrac{x^2}{2}\).

Dividing by \(x^2 > 0\) gives \(f(x) \leq \dfrac{1}{2}\) for \(x > 0\). Both \(1 - \cos x\) and \(x^2\) are unchanged when \(x\) is replaced by \(-x\), so the same holds for \(x < 0\); and \(f(0) = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{2xy}{x^2 + 3y^2}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the tangent to \(C\) at the point \(P(3, 1)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The tangent at P meets \(C\) again at the point Q. Find the coordinates of Q.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A particle moves along \(C\). When it passes through P, its \(x\)-coordinate is increasing at 2 units per second. Find the rate of change of its \(y\)-coordinate at that moment.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Show that \(0 < y \leq \sqrt[3]{10}\) at every point of \(C\).

idea: Use the product rule on \(x^2y\). For Q, substitute the tangent’s equation into the curve: the cubic in \(x\) must have a double root at \(x = 3\), because the line touches \(C\) there. For (e), factorise the left side as \(y(x^2 + y^2)\).

solution.label: c
steps: Substitute: \(\dfrac{x^2(5 - x)}{2} + \dfrac{(5 - x)^3}{8} = 10\). Multiply by 8 and simplify: \(-5x^3 + 35x^2 - 75x + 45 = 0\), that is \(x^3 - 7x^2 + 15x - 9 = 0\).
\(x = 3\) is a double root: \((x - 3)^2(x - 1) = 0\). So the other point has \(x = 1\), \(y = 2\). (Check: \(2 + 8 = 10\).)

solution.label: e
steps: Then \(y^3 \leq y(x^2 + y^2) = 10\), since \(yx^2 \geq 0\). So \(y \leq \sqrt[3]{10}\), with equality at \(x = 0\).

stem: Let \(I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin x}{\sin x + \cos x} \, dx\) and \(J = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos x}{\sin x + \cos x} \, dx\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the value of \(I + J\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the substitution \(u = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\) to show that \(I = J\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence write down the value of \(I\).
Let \(K = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} \ln(1 + \tan x) \, dx\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that \(1 + \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right) = \dfrac{2}{1 + \tan x}\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Use the substitution \(u = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\) to show that \(K = \dfrac{\pi}{8}\ln 2\).

parts.label: f
parts.text: Use the substitution \(x = \tan\theta\) to find the exact value of \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{\ln(1 + x)}{1 + x^2} \, dx\).

idea: Neither integral can be found directly. A substitution that reflects the interval (\(x \to \pi/2 - x\), or \(x \to \pi/4 - x\)) turns the integral into something related to itself, and an equation for the integral follows.

solution.label: b
steps: \(dx = -du\); \(x = 0 \to u = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \to u = 0\). \(\sin x = \cos u\), \(\cos x = \sin u\).
\(\displaystyle I = \int_{\pi/2}^{0} \frac{\cos u}{\cos u + \sin u}(-du) = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos u}{\sin u + \cos u} \, du = J\).

solution.label: d
steps: \(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right) = \dfrac{1 - \tan x}{1 + \tan x}\), so \(1 + \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right) = \dfrac{(1 + \tan x) + (1 - \tan x)}{1 + \tan x} = \dfrac{2}{1 + \tan x}\).

stem: The region \(R\) is enclosed by the curves \(y = 2\sin x\) and \(y = \tan x\), for \(0 \leq x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the curves meet at \(x = 0\) and \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), and at no other point with \(0 \leq x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the area of \(R\) is \(1 - \ln 2\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the exact volume of the solid formed when \(R\) is rotated through \(360°\) about the \(x\)-axis.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write down an integral with respect to \(y\) for the volume of the solid formed when \(R\) is rotated through \(360°\) about the \(y\)-axis, and find its value.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The line \(x = k\), where \(0 < k < \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), divides \(R\) into two parts of equal area. Find the value of \(k\).

idea: \(2\sin x = \tan x\) gives \(\sin x(2\cos x - 1) = 0\). On the region \(2\sin x \geq \tan x\), so the upper curve is \(2\sin x\). For a rotation about the \(y\)-axis, write each curve as \(x\) in terms of \(y\): \(x = \arcsin\dfrac{y}{2}\) and \(x = \arctan y\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(2\sin x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) gives \(\sin x\,(2\cos x - 1) = 0\). On \(0 \leq x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(\sin x = 0\) only at \(x = 0\), and \(\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}\) only at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

solution.label: b
steps: For \(0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), \(\cos x > \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(2\sin x > \tan x\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(\displaystyle V = \pi\int_0^{\pi/3} \left(4\sin^2 x - \tan^2 x\right) dx\), with \(4\sin^2 x = 2 - 2\cos 2x\) and \(\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1\).

solution.label: d
steps: For \(0 \leq y \leq \sqrt{3}\), the region runs from \(x = \arcsin\dfrac{y}{2}\) to \(x = \arctan y\).

solution.label: e
steps: Solve \(\displaystyle\int_0^{k} (2\sin x - \tan x) \, dx = \frac{1 - \ln 2}{2}\), that is \(2 - 2\cos k + \ln(\cos k) = 0.15342\ldots\): \(k = 0.59113\ldots\)

stem: A lake holds a population of \(P\) fish, \(t\) years after a fishing licence is introduced. A model for the population is \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.16P\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{800}\right) - 24\), where 24 fish per year are caught.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the two values of \(P\) for which the population does not change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.0002(P - 200)(600 - P)\), and hence state the values of \(P\) for which the population increases.
When the licence is introduced there are 400 fish.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve the differential equation to show that \(P = \dfrac{200 + 600\mathrm{e}^{0.08t}}{1 + \mathrm{e}^{0.08t}}\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the time it takes for the population to reach 550.

parts.label: e
parts.text: In a second lake with the same model, there are 150 fish when the licence is introduced. Show that this population dies out, and find the time it takes.

idea: Write the right side as a product of two factors, then separate the variables and use partial fractions: \(\dfrac{1}{(P - 200)(600 - P)} = \dfrac{1}{400}\left(\dfrac{1}{P - 200} + \dfrac{1}{600 - P}\right)\). Below 200 both factors keep the same signs, so the population keeps falling.

solution.label: b
steps: \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} > 0\) when the two factors have the same sign.

solution.label: c
steps: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dP}{(P - 200)(600 - P)} = \int 0.0002 \, dt\). With partial fractions: \(\dfrac{1}{400}\ln\left|\dfrac{P - 200}{600 - P}\right| = 0.0002t + C\).

solution.label: e
steps: For \(P < 200\), \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.0002(P - 200)(600 - P) < 0\), so \(P\) keeps decreasing and cannot climb back to 200.

With \(P(0) = 150\): \(\dfrac{200 - P}{600 - P} = \dfrac{50}{450}\mathrm{e}^{0.08t} = \dfrac{1}{9}\mathrm{e}^{0.08t}\). (The formula from (c) does not apply: the constant is different.) At \(P = 0\): \(\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{9}\mathrm{e}^{0.08t}\), so \(t = \dfrac{\ln 3}{0.08} = 13.73\ldots\)

stem: Consider the differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y^2 - x^2}{2xy}\), for \(x > 0\) and \(y > 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the substitution \(y = vx\) to show that \(x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -\dfrac{1 + v^2}{2v}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that the general solution is \(x^2 + y^2 = Ax\), where \(A\) is a constant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the particular solution that passes through \((1, 1)\), and describe the curve.

parts.label: d
parts.text: For a constant \(B\), the curve \(x^2 + y^2 = By\) is a circle with its centre on the \(y\)-axis. Show that, at any point with \(x > 0\), \(y > 0\) and \(x \neq y\) where such a circle meets a solution curve from part (b), the two curves cross at right angles.

idea: The equation is homogeneous: the right side depends only on \(\dfrac{y}{x}\). After separating, \(\displaystyle\int \frac{2v}{1 + v^2}\,dv = \ln(1 + v^2)\). Two curves cross at right angles when the product of their gradients at the crossing point is \(-1\).

solution.label: b
steps: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{2v}{1 + v^2}\,dv = -\int \frac{dx}{x}\), so \(\ln(1 + v^2) = -\ln x + C\), and \(1 + v^2 = \dfrac{A}{x}\) with \(A = \mathrm{e}^C\).

solution.label: c
solution.answer: \(x^2 + y^2 = 2x\): part of the circle with centre \((1, 0)\) and radius 1 (the part with \(y > 0\))

solution.label: d
steps: Circle \(x^2 + y^2 = By\): \(2x + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = B\dfrac{dy}{dx}\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2x}{B - 2y}\). On the circle \(B = \dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{y}\), so \(B - 2y = \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{y}\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2xy}{x^2 - y^2}\).
Product of the gradients: \(\dfrac{y^2 - x^2}{2xy} \times \dfrac{2xy}{x^2 - y^2} = -1\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: By writing \(\dfrac{1}{1 + t^2}\) as the sum of a geometric series and integrating from 0 to \(x\), show that \(\arctan x = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{x^5}{5} - \ldots\) for \(|x| < 1\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \(\arctan\dfrac{1}{2} + \arctan\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence, using the first two terms of the series for each arctan, find an approximation to \(\pi\) as a fraction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x - \arctan x}{x^3}\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series for \(\mathrm{e}^x\arctan x\) up to and including the term in \(x^3\).

idea: \(\dfrac{1}{1 + t^2} = 1 - t^2 + t^4 - \ldots\) is geometric with ratio \(-t^2\), valid for \(|t| < 1\). For a product of two series, multiply them and keep only the powers you need.

solution.label: b
steps: \(\tan(A + B) = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}}{1 - \frac{1}{6}} = \dfrac{5/6}{5/6} = 1\). Both angles are between 0 and \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), so the sum is between 0 and \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), and must be \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
